expectedRelation: Juvenile arc crust may contain dense lower-crustal components and therefore supports context-dependent rather than universally positive buoyancy candidates.
weightRationale: The claim limits overconfident buoyancy assignment and is not a numeric weight or threshold.
exceptions: Arc sections vary in composition, pressure-temperature history, and lower-crust retention or foundering.

expectedRelation: Some intra-oceanic arc systems can generate intermediate-composition crust with properties between normal oceanic and mature continental endmembers.
weightRationale: The claim supports an arc or juvenile continental-affinity candidate class without making it universal.
exceptions: Not every volcanic arc produces or preserves juvenile continental-affinity crust.

expectedRelation: Continental crustal thickness, seismic structure, composition, density, and anisotropy vary with tectonic province, permitting relative continental substrate and thickness candidates.
weightRationale: The global synthesis supports qualitative candidate dimensions but not Earth-average numerical calibration in WorldWright.
exceptions: Continental lower crust can be mafic and continental provinces overlap strongly in measured properties.

expectedRelation: M1A deep substrate candidates cannot infer exposed rock, weathered material, sediment cover, land, water, elevation, bathymetry, or terrain.
weightRationale: This is an authority firewall and contributes no scientific support weight to a material class.

expectedRelation: Pre-existing lithospheric structure can preserve strength contrasts and mechanical anisotropy that guide later deformation.
weightRationale: The claim supports resistance and orientation-unresolved inherited-grain candidates, never a final line geometry.
exceptions: Effective elastic thickness is a proxy and does not uniquely determine local rheology or exposed structure.

expectedRelation: Crust and uppermost lithosphere vary laterally in thickness, velocity, density, and lid structure, supporting separate candidate dimensions instead of a single universal rock label.
weightRationale: The authoritative Earth model supports heterogeneous candidate dimensions but not direct generated-world classification.
exceptions: Earth model resolution and data coverage vary regionally.

expectedRelation: Some magma-poor rifted margins contain exhumed continental lithospheric mantle between continental and normal oceanic crust.
weightRationale: The claim establishes a real candidate class but current radial Phase D and C evidence cannot decide when or where it occurs.
exceptions: Volcanic and magma-rich margins can follow different transition architectures.

expectedRelation: Normal oceanic crust supports a relatively thin mafic substrate candidate compared with typical continental crust, with substantial spreading-rate and thermal variation.
weightRationale: The synthesis supports relative candidate tendencies, not a fixed thickness value or a water-depth conclusion.
exceptions: Hotspot proximity, spreading rate, mantle composition, and magma supply can produce anomalously thick or thin oceanic crust.

expectedRelation: Oceanic plateaus can preserve oceanic-affinity seismic layering while being substantially thicker than normal ocean-basin crust.
weightRationale: The claim supports a plume-modified or high-melt thick mafic alternative without fixing its origin, geometry, or relief.
exceptions: Oceanic plateaus differ in formation mechanism, composition, and later tectonic modification.

expectedRelation: Continental extension can thin crust and lithosphere while inherited rheological structure controls segmentation and preferred deformation corridors.
weightRationale: The claim supports thin, weakened, and orientation-unresolved rift candidates without creating a final margin geometry.
exceptions: Rift outcomes vary with thermal state, composition, strain rate, magma supply, and inherited structure.

expectedRelation: Orogenic and convergent provinces can preserve relatively thickened crustal structure compared with extended provinces.
weightRationale: The claim supports a thickening tendency candidate but does not authorize relief, plateau height, or mountain geometry.
exceptions: Erosion, delamination, extension, thermal weakening, and inherited composition can modify thickened crust.

expectedRelation: High melt production during rifting can build thick, high-velocity mafic igneous crust at volcanic margins.
weightRationale: The claim supports a magmatically thickened mafic alternative while explicitly avoiding a universal plume or margin rule.
exceptions: Magma-poor margins and normal oceanic spreading do not require thick volcanic-margin crust.
